explanation_correct: TAF stands for Terminal Aerodrome Forecast — a forecast of expected weather within 5 statute miles of the airport terminal area, usually covering 24 to 30 hours.

explanation_distractors.B: TAF is not a frequency. It is a weather forecast for the airport area.
explanation_distractors.C: TAF has nothing to do with terrain files. It forecasts airport weather conditions.

source: FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide Appendix 3

question_text: What does "VLOS" stand for?
explanation_correct: VLOS stands for Visual Line of Sight — the requirement that the RPIC, the person manipulating the controls, or a VO must see the unmanned aircraft throughout the flight with unaided vision (except corrective lenses).

explanation_distractors.B: VLOS is not an operating standard level. It is a visual tracking requirement.
explanation_distractors.C: VLOS has nothing to do with launch systems. It requires visual contact with the drone.

source: FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide Appendix 3

question_text: What does "BVLOS" stand for?
explanation_correct: BVLOS stands for Beyond Visual Line of Sight — operating a drone when the crew cannot directly see it. This is not routine under Part 107 and generally requires a waiver.

explanation_distractors.B: BVLOS is not a location standard. It describes operating beyond the pilot's visual range.
explanation_distractors.C: BVLOS has nothing to do with landing. It means the drone is beyond unaided visual range.

source: FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide Appendix 3

question_text: What does "FRIA" stand for?
explanation_correct: FRIA stands for FAA-Recognized Identification Area — a defined area where a drone without Remote ID equipment may operate if it stays within the FRIA and within VLOS.

explanation_distractors.B: FRIA has nothing to do with instrument approaches. It is a Remote ID exception area.
explanation_distractors.C: FRIA is not a flight restriction zone. It allows non-Remote-ID drones to fly in a defined area.

source: FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide Appendix 3

question_text: What does "LAANC" stand for?

options.text: Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability.
Local Airspace Advisory and Navigation Control.

explanation_correct: LAANC stands for Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability — the FAA system that automates many controlled-airspace authorization requests near airports through approved UAS Service Suppliers.

explanation_distractors.B: LAANC is not an advisory service. It automates airspace authorization for drone pilots.
explanation_distractors.C: LAANC is available for all Part 107 pilots, not just non-commercial operations.

source: FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide Appendix 3

question_text: What does the "IMSAFE" checklist stand for?

options.text: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion.
Instrument, Maintenance, Safety, Aircraft, Fuel, Equipment.
Inspection, Mechanical, System, Alert, Frequency, Emergency.

explanation_correct: IMSAFE stands for Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion — a personal readiness checklist pilots use to self-assess fitness for duty before flying.

explanation_distractors.B: IMSAFE is a personal fitness checklist, not an equipment inspection list.
explanation_distractors.C: IMSAFE has nothing to do with mechanical systems. It assesses pilot personal readiness.

source: FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide Appendix 3

question_text: What does "SRM" stand for?
explanation_correct: SRM stands for Single-Pilot Resource Management — using all available resources (automation, checklists, other people) when one pilot is solely responsible for the operation.

explanation_distractors.B: SRM is not about route mapping. It is about managing all available resources as a single pilot.
explanation_distractors.C: SRM is not a review manual. It is a pilot resource management concept.

source: FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide Appendix 3

question_text: What is the Part 107 default rule for drone operations under 55 lb?

options.text: Part 107 is the default regulation for most non-recreational operations.
Part 101 applies to all drone operations under 55 lb.
No FAA regulation applies to drones under 55 lb.

explanation_correct: For drones under 55 lb, Part 107 is the default regulation for most non-recreational operations.

explanation_distractors.B: Part 101 covers recreational operations (the exception), not the default rule.
explanation_distractors.C: FAA regulations do apply to all drone operations in the National Airspace System.

question_text: What does sUAS stand for and what does it mean under Part 107?

options.text: Small Unmanned Aircraft System — generally a drone operation under 55 lb at takeoff.
Standard Unmanned Aerial System — any drone over 25 lb.
Supervised Unmanned Aircraft System — requires a co-pilot.

explanation_correct: sUAS stands for Small Unmanned Aircraft System. Under Part 107 it generally means a drone operation under 55 lb at takeoff.

explanation_distractors.B: The 'S' stands for 'small' and the weight limit is 55 lb, not 25 lb.
explanation_distractors.C: sUAS does not require a co-pilot — it refers only to the weight category.

question_text: What is a Remote PIC (RPIC) under Part 107?

options.text: Remote Pilot in Command. Must be designated before or during the flight and has final authority and responsibility for the operation.
A person who monitors airspace from the ground during the flight.
An FAA inspector who oversees drone operations.

explanation_correct: The RPIC is the Remote Pilot in Command, must be designated before or during the flight, and has final authority and responsibility for the operation.

explanation_distractors.B: That describes a Visual Observer (VO), not the RPIC.
explanation_distractors.C: The RPIC is the operator, not an FAA inspector.

question_text: What is the role of a Visual Observer (VO) under Part 107?

options.text: An optional crewmember who helps maintain awareness; must be able to see the aircraft and maintain effective communication with the RPIC.
A mandatory crewmember who must be present on every Part 107 flight.
The person primarily responsible for controlling the drone.

explanation_correct: The VO is optional, helps maintain situational awareness, must maintain VLOS of the aircraft, and must communicate effectively with the RPIC and person manipulating the controls.

explanation_distractors.B: The VO is optional under Part 107, not mandatory.
explanation_distractors.C: The person manipulating the controls operates the drone; the VO is an observer role.

question_text: What does VLOS mean and who must maintain it?

options.text: Visual Line of Sight. The RPIC, person manipulating the controls, or a VO must see the aircraft throughout the flight with unaided vision (corrective lenses allowed).
Video Line of Sight. The RPIC may use FPV goggles as the sole means of maintaining sight.
Visual Line of Sight. Only the RPIC must maintain it at all times.

explanation_correct: VLOS (Visual Line of Sight) requires the RPIC, person manipulating the controls, or a VO to maintain unaided visual sight of the aircraft. Corrective lenses are allowed; FPV-only is not.

explanation_distractors.B: FPV goggles alone do not satisfy the VLOS requirement.
explanation_distractors.C: A VO may fulfill the VLOS requirement, so the RPIC alone is not the only option.

question_text: What is BVLOS and is it routine under current Part 107?

options.text: Beyond Visual Line of Sight. Not routine — generally requires an FAA waiver or specific authorization.
Beyond Visual Line of Sight. Allowed any time as long as the RPIC holds a Part 107 certificate.
Beyond Visual Line of Sight. Allowed routinely at night.

explanation_correct: BVLOS is Beyond Visual Line of Sight. It is not a routine Part 107 operation and generally requires an FAA waiver or specific authorization.

explanation_distractors.B: A Part 107 certificate alone does not authorize BVLOS operations.
explanation_distractors.C: Night authorization does not extend to BVLOS operations.

question_text: Who must comply with Remote ID requirements?

options.text: Drones that are required to be registered or are registered must comply.
Only commercial operators flying in Class B airspace.
Remote ID is optional for drones under 25 lb.

explanation_correct: Drones that are required to be registered or are registered must comply with Remote ID. Compliance paths include a Standard Remote ID drone, a broadcast module, or operating in a FRIA.

explanation_distractors.B: Remote ID applies based on registration requirements, not airspace class alone.
explanation_distractors.C: Remote ID is not optional for registered drones regardless of weight.

question_text: What is a FRIA and what does it allow?

options.text: FAA-Recognized Identification Area. A defined area where a drone without Remote ID equipment may operate, as long as it stays within the FRIA and within VLOS.
Federal Remote Identification Authority. An agency that approves Remote ID hardware.
A temporary exemption that waives all Part 107 rules within a defined airspace.

explanation_correct: FRIA stands for FAA-Recognized Identification Area. Drones without Remote ID equipment may operate there as long as they stay within the FRIA and within VLOS.

explanation_distractors.B: FRIA is an area designation, not a government authority.
explanation_distractors.C: The FRIA only addresses Remote ID, not all Part 107 rules.

question_text: What is LAANC and how does it work?

options.text: Low Altitude Authorization and Notification Capability. An FAA/UAS Data Exchange capability that automates many controlled-airspace authorization requests near airports via FAA-approved UAS Service Suppliers.
A physical license issued by the FAA that authorizes permanent drone operations near airports.
A weather alert system for low-altitude drone pilots.

explanation_correct: LAANC automates many controlled-airspace authorization requests near airports through FAA-approved UAS Service Suppliers, enabling near real-time approvals.

explanation_distractors.B: LAANC is an automated digital process, not a physical license.
explanation_distractors.C: LAANC is an airspace authorization tool, not a weather service.

question_text: Under Part 107, which airspace classes require prior ATC authorization?

options.text: Class B, C, D airspace, and within the lateral boundaries of surface Class E designated for an airport.
Only Class B airspace requires prior authorization.
Class G airspace — all others are unrestricted for drones.

explanation_correct: Prior ATC authorization is required for Class B, C, D, and within the lateral boundaries of surface Class E designated for an airport.

explanation_distractors.B: Class C, D, and surface-designated Class E also require authorization, not only Class B.
explanation_distractors.C: Class G is uncontrolled and does not require authorization; the other classes do.

question_text: What is the difference between a waiver and a COA under Part 107?

options.text: A waiver permits deviating from specific Part 107 rules. A COA (Certificate of Waiver or Authorization) is typically used for public aircraft or certain Part 91/public safety operations, not the normal Part 107 pathway.
A COA is the same as a waiver — the terms are interchangeable.
A waiver is only for military drones; a COA is for commercial operators.

explanation_correct: A Part 107 waiver permits deviating from specific Part 107 rules. A COA is an authorization typically used for public aircraft or certain Part 91/public safety operations, not the normal Part 107 pathway.

explanation_distractors.B: They are not interchangeable — they serve different regulatory purposes.
explanation_distractors.C: Waivers are for civilian Part 107 operators who need rule deviation; neither is exclusively military.

question_text: Under current Part 107, when can you fly at night without a waiver?

options.text: If the RPIC completed the required knowledge test or training after April 6, 2021, and the drone has anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles.
Night flight is always prohibited without a waiver.
Anytime — nighttime restrictions were fully removed in 2021.

explanation_correct: Night operations are allowed under current Part 107 if the RPIC completed the required initial knowledge test or training after April 6, 2021, and the drone is equipped with anti-collision lighting visible for at least 3 statute miles.

explanation_distractors.B: Night waivers are no longer required if the pilot meets the current training requirement.
explanation_distractors.C: Lighting and training requirements still apply — night flight is not completely unrestricted.

question_text: Under Part 107, when are operations over people allowed without a waiver?

options.text: Only if the person is directly participating, under a covered structure, inside a stationary vehicle, or the operation meets Category 1, 2, 3, or 4 requirements.
Operations over people are always allowed below 400 ft AGL.
Operations over people require a waiver in all cases.

explanation_correct: Part 107 allows operations over people only for direct participants, those under covered structures, those in stationary vehicles, or when the operation fits Category 1, 2, 3, or 4. Category 3 cannot be used for open-air assemblies.

explanation_distractors.B: Altitude alone does not authorize operations over non-participating people.
explanation_distractors.C: Categories 1–4 provide waiver-free pathways for operations over people.

question_text: What is the maximum altitude under Part 107, and when does the 400 ft limit not apply?

options.text: Maximum is 400 ft AGL, unless within 400 ft of a structure — then you may fly up to 400 ft above that structure's uppermost limit.
Maximum is 400 ft AGL with no exceptions.
Maximum is 500 ft AGL unless in controlled airspace.

explanation_correct: The default max altitude is 400 ft AGL. When operating within 400 ft of a structure, the drone may fly up to 400 ft above the structure's immediate uppermost limit.

explanation_distractors.B: The structure exception is a real and important exception to the 400 ft AGL rule.
explanation_distractors.C: The limit is 400 ft AGL, not 500 ft.

question_text: What is the minimum flight visibility requirement under Part 107?

options.text: 3 statute miles as observed from the control station.
1 statute mile at any altitude below 400 ft AGL.
5 statute miles for operations in Class G airspace.

explanation_correct: The minimum flight visibility under Part 107 is 3 statute miles as observed from the control station.

explanation_distractors.B: 1 SM is below the required minimum — Part 107 requires at least 3 SM.
explanation_distractors.C: The standard is 3 SM regardless of airspace class (in uncontrolled Class G).

question_text: What are the minimum cloud clearance requirements under Part 107?

options.text: 500 ft below clouds and 2,000 ft horizontally from clouds.
Clear of clouds at all times.
1,000 ft below and 1,000 ft horizontally from clouds.

explanation_correct: Part 107 requires minimum cloud clearance of 500 ft below clouds and 2,000 ft horizontally from clouds.

explanation_distractors.B: 'Clear of clouds' is the VFR rule for Class B airspace, not the Part 107 standard.
explanation_distractors.C: 1,000 ft below and 1,000 ft horizontal are not the Part 107 minimums.

question_text: Under Part 107, what right-of-way rule applies to small unmanned aircraft?

options.text: Small unmanned aircraft must yield right of way to all aircraft, airborne vehicles, and launch and reentry vehicles.
Manned aircraft must yield to drones in controlled airspace.
Right of way is determined by who is operating at lower altitude.

explanation_correct: Under Part 107, small unmanned aircraft must yield right of way to all aircraft, airborne vehicles, and launch and reentry vehicles.

explanation_distractors.B: Drones always yield to manned aircraft, not the other way around.
explanation_distractors.C: Altitude does not determine right of way — drones always yield.

question_text: What preflight familiarization and inspection is required before a Part 107 flight?

options.text: Assess local weather, airspace and flight restrictions, nearby people and property, other ground hazards, and verify the aircraft is in a condition for safe operation.
Only verify the aircraft battery is charged.
No preflight is required for flights under 10 minutes.

explanation_correct: Before flight, the RPIC must assess local weather, airspace and flight restrictions, nearby people and property, other ground hazards, and verify the aircraft is in a condition for safe operation.

explanation_distractors.B: Preflight includes airspace, weather, and safety assessment — not just battery check.
explanation_distractors.C: Preflight requirements apply to every flight regardless of duration.

question_text: When must a drone accident be reported to the FAA under Part 107?

options.text: Within 10 calendar days if the operation causes serious injury, loss of consciousness, or more than $500 damage to property other than the drone.
Within 24 hours for any crash landing.
Only if an manned aircraft is involved.

explanation_correct: Report to the FAA within 10 calendar days if the operation causes serious injury, loss of consciousness, or more than $500 damage to property other than the drone.

explanation_distractors.B: The threshold is serious injury or over $500 property damage — not every crash landing.
explanation_distractors.C: The reporting requirement is not limited to incidents involving manned aircraft.

question_text: What alcohol rule applies to Part 107 pilots and Visual Observers?

options.text: Must comply with 14 CFR 91.17 and 91.19: 8-hour bottle-to-throttle rule and no alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater.
No numeric alcohol limit — just no visible impairment.
The 8-hour rule applies to the RPIC only, not the VO.

explanation_correct: Part 107 cross-references 14 CFR 91.17 and 91.19, requiring the 8-hour bottle-to-throttle rule and no blood alcohol concentration of 0.04 or greater. This applies to the RPIC, person manipulating controls, and VO.

explanation_distractors.B: There is a numeric limit of 0.04 blood alcohol concentration.
explanation_distractors.C: The alcohol rule applies to all crew, including VOs.

question_text: What is a NOTAM and what does it stand for?

options.text: Notice to Airmen. Time-critical notices about abnormal changes or hazards in the National Airspace System.
Notice to Air Missions. Permanent announcements about airports.
National Observation and Tracking Alert Message.

explanation_correct: NOTAM stands for Notice to Airmen. These are time-critical notices about abnormal changes or hazards in the National Airspace System. (FAA Order JO 7930.2U changed the current usage back to Notice to Airmen in 2025.)

explanation_distractors.B: 'Notice to Air Missions' was a previous term. The current FAA order reverted to 'Notice to Airmen' in 2025.
explanation_distractors.C: That is not a real FAA term.

question_text: What is an FDC NOTAM?

options.text: A Flight Data Center NOTAM — a regulatory NOTAM type. Temporary Flight Restrictions are issued as FDC NOTAMs.
A Federal Defense Command NOTAM issued for military airspace.
A local NOTAM issued by the airport tower.

explanation_correct: FDC stands for Flight Data Center. FDC NOTAMs are regulatory in nature. Temporary Flight Restrictions (TFRs) are issued as FDC NOTAMs.

explanation_distractors.B: FDC stands for Flight Data Center, not Federal Defense Command.
explanation_distractors.C: FDC NOTAMs are issued nationally, not by local towers.

question_text: What is a TFR?

options.text: Temporary Flight Restriction. A temporary airspace restriction commonly issued by FDC NOTAM for security, VIP movement, disasters, major events, or safety.
Terminal Flight Route. A published route near an airport.
Traffic Flow Restriction issued by the tower controller.

explanation_correct: TFR stands for Temporary Flight Restriction, a temporary airspace restriction issued by FDC NOTAM. Common reasons include security, VIP movements, disasters, major events, and safety.

explanation_distractors.B: There is no FAA term 'Terminal Flight Route'.
explanation_distractors.C: TFRs are issued nationally via FDC NOTAM, not by individual tower controllers.

question_text: What is the format of the UAG Remote Pilot knowledge test?

options.text: 60 questions, 2.0 hours allowed, 70 percent passing score.
80 questions, 3.0 hours allowed, 75 percent passing score.
40 questions, 1.0 hour allowed, 70 percent passing score.

explanation_correct: The UAG Remote Pilot knowledge test has 60 questions, a 2.0-hour time limit, and a 70 percent passing score, as listed in the current FAA testing matrix.

explanation_distractors.B: The test has 60 questions, not 80, and 2.0 hours, not 3.0.
explanation_distractors.C: The test has 60 questions and 2.0 hours, not 40 questions and 1.0 hour.

question_text: Which FAA testing supplement is currently listed for the UAG Remote Pilot exam?

options.text: FAA-CT-8080-2H (2018), used for the figures and charts on the UAG exam.

explanation_correct: The current FAA testing matrix still points Remote Pilot applicants to FAA-CT-8080-2H (2018) for the figures and charts used on the UAG exam.

explanation_distractors.B: FAA-CT-8080-3F is not the supplement for the UAG test.
explanation_distractors.C: FAA-CT-8080-9A is not the supplement for the UAG test.

question_text: What does AGL mean in aviation?

options.text: Above Ground Level — height measured from the surface directly below the aircraft.
Altitude Guidance Limit — the ceiling set by ATC.
Aeronautical Ground Level — MSL corrected for terrain.

explanation_correct: AGL stands for Above Ground Level. It is height measured from the surface directly below the aircraft — not from sea level.

explanation_distractors.B: AGL is a measurement reference, not a limit set by ATC.
explanation_distractors.C: AGL measures from the surface below; MSL measures from sea level.

question_text: What does MSL mean in aviation?

options.text: Mean Sea Level — many charted altitudes and airspace floors/ceilings are expressed in MSL.
Minimum Safe Level — the lowest permitted flight altitude.
Maximum Speed Limit — maximum airspeed near airports.

explanation_correct: MSL stands for Mean Sea Level. Many charted altitudes and airspace floors and ceilings are expressed as MSL values.

explanation_distractors.B: MSL is a reference datum, not a regulatory floor.
explanation_distractors.C: MSL has nothing to do with airspeed limits.

question_text: What is a METAR?

options.text: Meteorological Aerodrome Report — current airport weather observation, usually issued hourly.
A 24-hour weather forecast for terminal areas.

explanation_correct: METAR is a Meteorological Aerodrome Report. It is the current airport weather observation, usually issued every hour.

explanation_distractors.B: METAR is a civilian weather reporting format, not a military one.
explanation_distractors.C: A 24-hour forecast is a TAF, not a METAR.

question_text: What is a TAF?

options.text: Terminal Aerodrome Forecast — forecast of expected weather within 5 SM of the airport terminal area, usually for 24 or 30 hours.
Turbulence Alert Forecast — warnings for severe turbulence.
Temperature and Frontal chart issued daily by the NWS.

explanation_correct: TAF stands for Terminal Aerodrome Forecast. It is a forecast of expected weather within 5 statute miles of the airport, usually covering 24 hours (sometimes 30 hours).

explanation_distractors.B: Turbulence warnings are issued as AIRMETs or SIGMETs, not TAFs.
explanation_distractors.C: TAF is a forecast product, not a chart product.

question_text: What is an AIRMET?

options.text: Advisory for significant weather affecting aircraft operations at intensities lower than a SIGMET — examples include IFR conditions, mountain obscuration, turbulence, icing.
An emergency weather alert for all aircraft regardless of type.
A routine hourly weather broadcast at airports with ATIS.

explanation_correct: An AIRMET (Airmen's Meteorological Information) advises of significant weather at intensities lower than those requiring a SIGMET. Examples include IFR conditions, mountain obscuration, turbulence, strong surface winds, icing, and freezing levels.

explanation_distractors.B: SIGMETs cover more severe weather hazards significant to all aircraft.
explanation_distractors.C: ATIS broadcasts are local; AIRMETs are area-wide weather advisories.

question_text: What is a SIGMET?

options.text: Weather advisory significant to the safety of all aircraft, covering hazards such as severe turbulence, severe icing, and widespread dust or sandstorms reducing visibility below 3 miles.
A signal-based meteorological alert sent via radio.
A low-level weather advisory for small drones only.

explanation_correct: A SIGMET (Significant Meteorological Information) is a weather advisory significant to the safety of all aircraft. It covers hazards such as severe turbulence, severe icing, and widespread dust/sandstorms reducing visibility below 3 miles.

explanation_distractors.B: SIGMETs are textual weather products, not radio signals.
explanation_distractors.C: SIGMETs affect all aircraft, not just drones.

question_text: What are AWOS and ASOS?

options.text: Automated weather systems at airports that collect and disseminate airport weather information.
Air traffic control communication frequencies for weather broadcasts.

explanation_correct: AWOS (Automated Weather Observing System) and ASOS (Automated Surface Observing System) are automated weather systems at airports that collect and disseminate airport weather information.

explanation_distractors.B: AWOS/ASOS are weather observation systems, not communication frequencies.
explanation_distractors.C: Both are ground-based airport systems, not satellites.

question_text: What is a CTAF?

options.text: Common Traffic Advisory Frequency — used for airport advisory practices at airports without an operating control tower.
Control Tower Approach Frequency — assigned by ATC for instrument approaches.
Commercial Traffic Announcement Frequency for airline operations.

explanation_correct: CTAF (Common Traffic Advisory Frequency) is used at airports without an operating control tower. The CTAF may be a UNICOM, MULTICOM, FSS, or tower frequency.

explanation_distractors.B: Instrument approach frequencies are assigned by ATC, not called CTAF.
explanation_distractors.C: CTAF is not commercial-specific; it is for any aircraft at non-towered airports.

question_text: What is UNICOM?

options.text: A nongovernment communication facility that may provide airport information at certain airports. Locations and frequencies are shown on aeronautical charts.
A universal emergency communication system for all aircraft.
The ATC tower frequency at Class D airports.

explanation_correct: UNICOM is a nongovernment communication facility that may provide airport information at certain airports. Its locations and frequencies are shown on aeronautical charts and publications.

explanation_distractors.B: Emergency communications use Guard frequency (121.5 MHz), not UNICOM.
explanation_distractors.C: Class D airports have an ATC tower with an assigned frequency, not UNICOM.

question_text: What is MULTICOM?

options.text: A mobile service for communications essential to private aircraft activities — commonly used for self-announce where no tower or UNICOM is available.
A frequency used only for drone operators near uncontrolled airports.

explanation_correct: MULTICOM is a mobile service used for communications essential to private aircraft activities. In pilot training, it is the self-announce option where no tower or UNICOM is available.

explanation_distractors.B: MULTICOM is a designated frequency, not an ATC system.
explanation_distractors.C: MULTICOM is used by all general aviation, not exclusively by drone operators.

question_text: What is ATIS?

options.text: Automatic Terminal Information Service — continuous broadcast of recorded noncontrol information in selected high-activity terminal areas.
Air Traffic Information System — the computer system tracking radar targets.
Advanced Tower Instruction Sequence used at busy Class B airports.

explanation_correct: ATIS is the Automatic Terminal Information Service, providing a continuous broadcast of recorded noncontrol information such as weather, NOTAMs, and active runways at high-activity terminal areas.

explanation_distractors.B: Radar tracking systems have different names; ATIS is an audio broadcast.
explanation_distractors.C: ATIS is a passive information broadcast, not a sequencing system.

question_text: What is an FSS?

options.text: Flight Service Station — provides pilot briefings, flight plan processing, search and rescue help, weather, NOTAM processing, and aeronautical information.
Federal Surveillance System — radar monitoring network.
Flight Safety System — the black box recorder on manned aircraft.

explanation_correct: FSS (Flight Service Station) is an air traffic facility that provides pilot briefings, flight plan processing, search and rescue assistance, weather, NOTAM processing, and aeronautical information.

explanation_distractors.B: FSS is a human-staffed information service, not a radar system.
explanation_distractors.C: Black box recorders are flight data recorders (FDR), not FSS.

question_text: What is a MOA?

options.text: Military Operations Area — airspace outside Class A to separate certain nonhazardous military activities from IFR traffic and identify the area for VFR pilots.
Mandatory Operations Airspace requiring ATC clearance.
A restricted area where all civilian flight is prohibited.

explanation_correct: MOA (Military Operations Area) is airspace established outside Class A to separate certain nonhazardous military activities from IFR traffic and to identify the area for VFR pilots.

explanation_distractors.B: MOAs do not require ATC clearance for VFR pilots, though caution is advised.
explanation_distractors.C: MOAs are advisory for VFR traffic; they are not prohibited areas.

question_text: What is an MTR?

options.text: Military Training Route — airspace of defined vertical and lateral dimensions used for military training at airspeeds greater than 250 knots.
Mandatory Traffic Route near Class B airports.
Metropolitan Terminal Region — a wide-area airspace designation.

explanation_correct: MTR (Military Training Route) is airspace of defined vertical and lateral dimensions established for military training at airspeeds greater than 250 knots indicated airspeed.

explanation_distractors.B: MTRs are military training routes, not mandatory civilian traffic routes.
explanation_distractors.C: MTR is a specific airspace type, not a metropolitan designation.

question_text: What is TPA and what is the standard value?

options.text: Traffic Pattern Altitude — standard is usually 1,000 ft AGL for most propeller aircraft unless otherwise published.
Terminal Procedures Altitude — the minimum approach altitude.
Tower Pattern Approach — the altitude at which the tower clears aircraft to land.

explanation_correct: TPA stands for Traffic Pattern Altitude. Standard TPA for most propeller aircraft is 1,000 ft AGL unless otherwise published. Drone pilots should stay alert for aircraft using the airport pattern.

explanation_distractors.B: Minimum approach altitudes are called MDA or DA, not TPA.
explanation_distractors.C: TPA is a published pattern altitude, not a clearance altitude.

question_text: When using aviation weather reports and charts, what unit is used for visibility versus distances?

options.text: Statute miles (SM) for weather visibility; nautical miles (NM) for aviation distance and speed references such as knots.
Nautical miles for everything in aviation.
Kilometers for weather visibility; miles for navigation.

explanation_correct: Statute miles (SM) are used for weather visibility reporting. Nautical miles (NM) are used for aviation distance and speed references (knots).

explanation_distractors.B: Visibility is reported in statute miles, not nautical miles.
explanation_distractors.C: U.S. aviation uses miles and nautical miles, not kilometers.

question_text: What is density altitude and how does it affect performance?

options.text: Pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature. High density altitude reduces lift, climb performance, and battery margin.
The altitude at which an aircraft must fly for maximum fuel efficiency.
The altitude measured from sea level based on air density alone.

explanation_correct: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature. High density altitude (hot, high, humid conditions) reduces lift, climb performance, and often battery margin for electric drones.

explanation_distractors.B: Density altitude is a performance indicator, not an efficiency altitude.
explanation_distractors.C: Density altitude combines pressure and temperature effects — it is not simply an MSL reading.

question_text: What is ADM in aviation?

options.text: Aeronautical Decision Making — systematic process for identifying hazards, assessing risk, and choosing safe actions.
Aircraft Diagnostics and Maintenance — the preflight checklist system.
Altitude Deviation Monitoring — an autopilot function.

explanation_correct: ADM (Aeronautical Decision Making) is the systematic process for identifying hazards, assessing risk, and choosing safe actions during a flight operation.

explanation_distractors.B: Preflight checklists are separate from ADM; ADM is about decision-making processes.
explanation_distractors.C: Altitude deviation monitoring is an autopilot feature, not ADM.

question_text: What does PAVE stand for?

options.text: A risk checklist: Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures.

explanation_correct: PAVE is a risk identification checklist: Pilot (fitness), Aircraft (airworthiness), enVironment (weather and airspace), External pressures (get-there-itis and schedule pressure).

explanation_distractors.B: That is not a real FAA acronym.
explanation_distractors.C: That is not the PAVE definition.

question_text: What does IMSAFE stand for?

options.text: Personal readiness checklist: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion.
Instrument Meteorological Safety and Flight Evaluation.
In-Mission Safety and Flight Emergency checklist.

explanation_correct: IMSAFE is a personal readiness checklist: Illness, Medication, Stress, Alcohol, Fatigue, Emotion. Pilots use it to self-assess fitness before each flight.

explanation_distractors.B: IMSAFE is a personal readiness checklist, not an instrument weather evaluation.
explanation_distractors.C: IMSAFE is a preflight personal assessment, not an in-flight emergency checklist.

question_text: What is SRM?

options.text: Single-Pilot Resource Management — using all available resources when one pilot is responsible for the operation.
Standard Route Management — the FAA flight planning protocol.
Safety Risk Management — the formal SMS process.

explanation_correct: SRM (Single-Pilot Resource Management) is the effective use of all available resources — information, automation, crew — when one pilot bears sole responsibility for the operation.

explanation_distractors.B: SRM is about in-flight resource use, not a route planning protocol.
explanation_distractors.C: Safety Risk Management is part of a Safety Management System (SMS), not SRM.

question_text: What is CRM?

options.text: Crew Resource Management — effective use of people, equipment, and information to improve safety and decision making.
Critical Response Methodology for emergency procedures.

explanation_correct: CRM (Crew Resource Management) is the effective use of all available resources — people, equipment, and information — to improve safety and decision making in flight operations.

explanation_distractors.B: Radio management is one element of CRM, not its definition.
explanation_distractors.C: CRM is a broad operational philosophy, not only for emergencies.

question_text: What is the Center of Gravity (CG) in aviation?

options.text: The balance point of the aircraft system. An improper CG can degrade stability and performance.
The geometric center of the aircraft's fuselage.

explanation_correct: CG (Center of Gravity) is the balance point of the aircraft system. If the CG is outside allowable limits it can degrade stability, handling, and performance.

explanation_distractors.B: Maximum takeoff weight is a separate specification from CG.
explanation_distractors.C: CG is the balance point based on weight distribution, not the geometric center.

question_text: What is Load Factor?

options.text: The ratio of aerodynamic load supported by the aircraft to the aircraft's weight. Higher load factor increases aerodynamic demand during maneuvering.
The maximum payload the aircraft can carry.
The ratio of battery capacity to flight time.

explanation_correct: Load factor is the ratio of aerodynamic load supported by the wings or rotors to the aircraft's weight. Higher load factors occur during turns and maneuvering and increase aerodynamic demand.

explanation_distractors.B: Payload capacity is a separate specification. Load factor is a ratio, not a weight.
explanation_distractors.C: Load factor is an aerodynamic concept, not a battery metric.

question_text: When would you use the Sectional Chart Legend on the FAA exam?

options.text: The legend is the chart symbol cheat sheet. It is worth knowing how to flip to it quickly when a figure has an unfamiliar symbol.
The legend is never needed on the exam because all symbols are explained in the question text.
The legend is only used for IFR charts, not sectional charts.

explanation_correct: The sectional chart legend is the symbol cheat sheet used during the exam. Knowing how to quickly reference it for unfamiliar chart symbols can save time on figure-heavy questions.

explanation_distractors.B: The exam does include figure questions with symbols that require the legend.
explanation_distractors.C: Sectional charts are VFR charts; the legend is for those charts specifically.

question_text: You are flying a small unmanned aircraft at night and observe an airplane flying at low altitude in your area. How can you determine if the aircraft is getting closer or moving farther away?

options.text: The aircraft will appear to be descending as it moves closer.
The lights on the aircraft will increase or decrease in intensity.
The aircraft's lights will appear to change colors.

explanation_correct: At night, an aircraft that is getting closer will generally appear brighter because its lights increase in intensity. Dimming lights usually indicate the aircraft is moving farther away.

explanation_distractors.A: Relative descent alone is not a reliable nighttime cue for whether another aircraft is closing on your position.
explanation_distractors.C: Navigation light colors indicate aircraft orientation, not whether it is getting closer or farther away.

question_text: Why would it be unsafe to operate a small unmanned aircraft in the vicinity of hot air balloons?

options.text: Because of the unpredictability caused by wind.
Because of the Coriolis effect caused by the Earth's rotation.
Because hot air balloons may be tethered during launch, landing, or ground handling, and the tethered lines can be extremely difficult to see.

explanation_correct: Hot air balloons can be tethered during launch, landing, or ground handling. Those lines can be extremely difficult to detect from a remote pilot station, creating a severe collision hazard for a small UAS.

explanation_distractors.A: Wind affects balloons, but the specific hazard described here is the presence of nearly invisible tether lines.
explanation_distractors.B: The Coriolis effect does not create the immediate operational hazard that tether lines do in the launch and recovery area.

question_text: Two certified remote pilots want to transfer control of a small UA during active flight. How may this be accomplished?

options.text: There can only be one remote pilot who maintains control and authority at a time during the transfer.
By sharing the control responsibility at the same time.
Only by landing the aircraft before transferring control.

explanation_correct: Only one person may act as remote PIC at a time. Control may be transferred during flight, but a single remote pilot must maintain operational authority and responsibility throughout the handoff.

explanation_distractors.B: Part 107 does not allow shared simultaneous command authority over the same aircraft.
explanation_distractors.C: Landing is not required if the transfer is managed so that one remote pilot clearly holds authority at all times.

question_text: If a remote PIC intentionally falsifies a required report, what action may the FAA take?

options.text: Issue only a warning letter unless property damage occurred.
Suspend or revoke any certificate, waiver, or declaration of compliance.
Require the remote PIC to retake the knowledge test within 30 days.

explanation_correct: Under Part 107, falsification, reproduction, or alteration of applications, certificates, logbooks, reports, or records can lead the FAA to suspend or revoke a certificate, waiver, or declaration of compliance.

explanation_distractors.A: Intentional falsification is not limited to a warning letter and is not conditioned on property damage.
explanation_distractors.C: The regulation authorizes certificate, waiver, or declaration action, not a simple retest requirement.

question_text: While flying a small unmanned aircraft forward, nearby trees appear to move quickly while distant mountains appear to move slowly. This is an example of
explanation_correct: Motion parallax is the apparent difference in rate of movement of objects at different distances. Nearby objects seem to move faster than distant objects as the aircraft moves forward.

explanation_distractors.B: Autokinesis is the illusion that a stationary light is moving when stared at in darkness.
explanation_distractors.C: The Coriolis illusion is a vestibular illusion caused by head movement during acceleration, not by relative motion of near and far objects.

question_text: A remote PIC correctly identifies all hazards in the operating environment and understands how these hazards could affect the flight outcome. This best describes
explanation_correct: Situational awareness is the accurate perception and understanding of all factors affecting the operation, including hazards and how they may change the flight outcome.

explanation_distractors.A: Risk management is the process of identifying and mitigating hazards, but the question describes the pilot's accurate understanding of the current operating picture.
explanation_distractors.B: ADM is the broader decision-making process. Situational awareness is a key input to ADM.

question_text: A remote pilot plans to operate a small unmanned aircraft system within Class B airspace. Which of the following is required for the operation?

options.text: The aircraft must be equipped with ADS-B Out.
The remote PIC must obtain ATC authorization before operating in Class B airspace.
The aircraft must be equipped with a Mode C transponder.

explanation_correct: Part 107 operations in Class B airspace require prior ATC authorization. Small UAS are not required to carry ADS-B Out or a Mode C transponder for this purpose.

explanation_distractors.A: ADS-B Out is not a standard requirement for Part 107 operations in Class B airspace.
explanation_distractors.C: A Mode C transponder is not required for a small UAS under Part 107 to obtain authorization.

question_text: What precautions should a remote PIC take to reduce the risk of flight emergencies when using lithium-based batteries?

options.text: Use batteries that show signs of swelling.
Follow the manufacturer's charging and temperature guidelines.

explanation_correct: Lithium-based batteries should be charged, stored, and used according to the manufacturer's temperature and charging guidance. That reduces the risk of battery failure, fire, or in-flight power loss.

explanation_distractors.A: Fully discharging lithium batteries can damage them and may increase failure risk depending on the battery type.
explanation_distractors.B: Swelling is a warning sign of battery damage and should be treated as an unsafe condition.

question_text: Which situation best represents an external pressure affecting decision-making during a remote pilot operation?

options.text: The desire to complete a paid flight on time.

explanation_correct: External pressures include schedule demands, client expectations, financial incentives, and self-imposed pressure to complete a mission even when conditions suggest delaying or canceling it.

explanation_distractors.A: Poor weather is an operational hazard, not an external pressure.
explanation_distractors.C: Equipment malfunction is a mechanical issue, not a pressure on the pilot's decision-making.

question_text: When an altimeter setting is adjusted to 29.92 inches of mercury, what altitude is being displayed?
explanation_correct: Setting 29.92 inches of mercury in the altimeter window causes the instrument to indicate pressure altitude, which is the altitude above the standard datum plane.

explanation_distractors.A: True altitude is the aircraft's actual height above mean sea level after correcting for nonstandard conditions.
explanation_distractors.B: Density altitude is pressure altitude corrected for nonstandard temperature.

question_text: During a complex drone operation, a visual observer notices another aircraft approaching the operation area but hesitates to inform the remote pilot because they assume the PIC already sees it. This situation best illustrates a breakdown in
explanation_correct: Crew resource management depends on timely, assertive communication among all participants. Hesitating to speak up about an approaching aircraft is a CRM breakdown.

explanation_distractors.A: Situational awareness may degrade as a result, but the root failure described is the crew's poor coordination and communication.
explanation_distractors.C: ADM is the broader decision process; the scenario specifically describes a crew communication problem.

question_text: What visual scanning method should a remote pilot use to effectively detect other aircraft and avoid collisions?

options.text: Stare at one point in the distance and wait for movement.
Use a series of short, regularly spaced eye movements to scan small sections of the sky.

explanation_correct: Effective visual scanning uses short, deliberate eye movements that divide the sky into small sections. That allows the eyes time to focus and improves the chance of detecting conflicting traffic.

explanation_distractors.A: Fixating on one point reduces overall traffic detection and can cause conflicting aircraft to be missed.
explanation_distractors.C: Peripheral vision alone is not reliable for see-and-avoid duties.

question_text: As a remote pilot, long extended flights during hot summer temperatures increase the susceptibility to dehydration because

options.text: hot days increase the rate of water loss in the body.
body water loss slows as long as the pilot remains seated at the controls.
the body's need for water decreases in hot weather.

explanation_correct: High temperatures increase perspiration and fluid loss. Without active hydration, a remote pilot is more susceptible to dehydration, fatigue, and degraded judgment.

explanation_distractors.B: Remaining seated does not prevent heat-related fluid loss.
explanation_distractors.C: Hot weather increases, not decreases, the body's need for water.

question_text: A remote pilot receives LAANC authorization for controlled airspace but launches 15 minutes earlier than the approved start time due to favorable weather. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The authorization remains valid as long as the altitude limits are followed.
The operation is unauthorized during the unapproved time window.
Early operations are allowed if ATC is not actively monitoring.

explanation_correct: ATC authorization through LAANC is limited to the approved date, time window, and altitude. Launching before the authorized start time is outside the authorization and is therefore not permitted.

explanation_distractors.A: Altitude limits are only one part of the authorization; the approved time window also governs the operation.
explanation_distractors.C: Authorization requirements do not depend on whether ATC is actively monitoring the flight.

question_text: During a Part 107 operation, the remote PIC deviates from a regulation to avoid an unexpected manned helicopter that enters the operating area. What must the remote PIC do after the flight?

options.text: Nothing, because emergency authority permanently resolves the situation.
Submit a written report to the FAA only if requested.
Immediately notify air traffic control after landing.

explanation_correct: In an in-flight emergency, the remote PIC may deviate from Part 107 rules to the extent needed to respond safely. The FAA may then require a written report of that deviation on request.

explanation_distractors.A: Emergency authority does not eliminate possible follow-up reporting if the FAA asks for it.
explanation_distractors.C: Immediate ATC notification after landing is not the rule-based reporting requirement described in Part 107.

question_text: A remote pilot launches a Part 107 operation using a manufacturer-provided automated flight mode. The aircraft independently adjusts altitude to maintain tracking accuracy and briefly exceeds the authorized altitude without pilot input or warning. Who is responsible for the deviation?

options.text: No one, because the altitude change was automatic.

explanation_correct: The remote PIC remains directly responsible for the operation of the small UAS at all times, including when manufacturer-provided automation or autonomous features are being used.

explanation_distractors.A: Manufacturers provide features, but operational compliance remains the responsibility of the remote PIC.
explanation_distractors.C: Automation does not remove pilot responsibility under Part 107.

question_text: During a Part 107 operation, may a visual observer (VO) assume control of the small unmanned aircraft during flight?

options.text: Yes, at any time, if the remote pilot in command authorizes it
Yes, but only in an emergency situation
No, a visual observer may not manipulate the flight controls

explanation_correct: Answer sourced from FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide.

question_text: In small unmanned aircraft operations, what best describes the control station?

options.text: The physical location where the remote pilot stands while monitoring the flight
The ground-based control equipment used by the remote pilot to operate the small unmanned aircraft at the pilot's location
The launch and recovery area designated for the sUAS operation

explanation_correct: Answer sourced from FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide.

question_text: Which statement is correct regarding a small UAS operation during an in-flight emergency?

options.text: The remote pilot in command must immediately terminate the flight, regardless of surrounding hazards.
The remote pilot in command may deviate from Part 107 rules to avoid collision with a manned aircraft.
The remote pilot in command must get ATC approval before deviating from a rule.

explanation_correct: Answer sourced from FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide.

question_text: You purchased an older drone that does not have Standard Remote ID and weighs more than 250 grams. What is required to legally fly the drone in Class G airspace?

options.text: An internet connection to transmit Remote ID data

explanation_correct: Answer sourced from 14 CFR Part 89.

question_text: If you are planning to fly your small unmanned aircraft and the cloud ceiling is 600 feet AGL, what is the maximum altitude you may legally fly?
explanation_correct: Answer sourced from FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide.

question_text: When may a remote pilot operate a small unmanned aircraft during civil twilight?

options.text: With anti-collision lights visible for 3 SM
With anti-collision lights visible for at least 3 SM and flashing
With anti-collision lights flashing and visible for 1 statute mile

explanation_correct: Answer sourced from 14 CFR Sec. 107.29.

question_text: A remote pilot is conducting a small unmanned aircraft operation over open farmland. A visual observer (VO) is assisting the remote pilot by tracking the aircraft using binoculars to maintain visual line of sight. Is this operation compliant with Part 107?

options.text: Yes, a visual observer may use binoculars to maintain visual line of sight
Yes, as long as the remote pilot can see the aircraft at all times
No, a visual observer must maintain visual line of sight using unaided vision

explanation_correct: Answer sourced from FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide.

question_text: A visual observer (VO) sees a manned aircraft approaching the small unmanned aircraft but fails to notify the remote pilot in command (RPIC). What is the RPIC's responsibility in this situation?

options.text: The RPIC is still responsible for avoiding the manned aircraft and must take immediate action
The VO's failure relieves the RPIC of responsibility
The RPIC may continue the operation since the VO saw the aircraft

explanation_correct: Answer sourced from FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide.

question_text: After the preflight briefing, the remote pilot in command (RPIC) realizes they forgot to inform the crew that the small unmanned aircraft will not use obstacle avoidance systems due to the nature of the operation. What should the RPIC do?

options.text: Proceed with the operation since the crew is already briefed
Stop and update the briefing to ensure the crew understands the limitation
Rely on the crew to notice obstacles and adjust accordingly

explanation_correct: Answer sourced from FAA Remote Pilot Study Guide.

question_text: For Part 107 operations, civil twilight is defined as which of the following time periods?

options.text: When the sun is between 0 degrees and 6 degrees below the horizon
30 minutes before sunrise and 30 minutes after sunset
Any time the sky is partially illuminated

explanation_correct: Answer sourced from 14 CFR Sec. 107.29.

question_text: Who is responsible for ensuring a small UAS is properly equipped for night or civil twilight operations?
explanation_correct: Answer sourced from 14 CFR Sec. 107.29.

question_text: Under 14 CFR Sec. 89.130, what must an operator of a foreign-registered unmanned aircraft do before operating in U.S. airspace?

options.text: Register the aircraft with the FAA under Part 48
Obtain a Confirmation of Identification and keep it at the control station
Display the aircraft's registration number on the exterior

explanation_correct: Answer sourced from 14 CFR Sec. 89.130.
